overview: This file concerns U.S. inquiries into reduced transpacific press-communication rates involving Japan. The principal despatch reports that an October 1929 agreement, promoted by the Pacific Cable Company and the Radio Corporation of America in consultation with the Japanese Government, reduced the regular press rate from 36 to 18 cents per word and introduced a deferred rate of 9 cents shortly before the Institute of Pacific Relations conference at Kyoto. Follow-up correspondence shows that neither the Department of Commerce, the Federal Radio Commission, nor the Interstate Commerce Commission could confirm the report. A separate internal note records the amicable settlement of a dispute with a Japanese radio station over the 19.8-kilocycle frequency and requests that no diplomatic representations be made.

subfiles.title: Despatch from Neville on reduced press rates between Japan and the United States
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the results of an investigation into George H. Blakeslee's claim that the Japanese Government induced press organizations to accept sharply reduced deferred cable rates.
subfiles.summary: Neville reports that an agreement was reached in New York City on October 15, 1929, through the efforts of the Pacific Cable Company and the Radio Corporation of America in telegraphic consultation with the Japanese Government. It reduced the regular press rate from 36 to 18 cents per word and established a new deferred press rate of 9 cents. The rates were announced shortly before the Institute of Pacific Relations conference opened at Kyoto, and Neville explains that Blakeslee's phrase “press organizations” apparently referred to the news agencies and associations represented in Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department inquiry to the Secretary of Commerce
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Acting Secretary of State, by an unnamed Assistant Secretary
subfiles.about: Forwards Neville's despatch and asks the Department of Commerce for information confirming the reported reduction of press rates from Japan.
subfiles.summary: The State Department transmits a copy of despatch No. 1395 from the American Embassy in Tokyo. It asks whether the Department of Commerce possesses information that might confirm the reported agreement reducing regular press rates and creating a deferred press rate from Japan.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department reply concerning press-rate inquiries
subfiles.from: E. M. Morgan, Acting Secretary of Commerce
subfiles.about: Reports that the Commerce Department and two federal commissions lack information confirming the press-rate agreement.
subfiles.summary: Morgan acknowledges receipt of the State Department's letter and Neville's despatch but states that the Department of Commerce has no information on the reported agreement. Inquiries to the Federal Radio Commission and Interstate Commerce Commission produced the same result. He notes that the office's only related correspondence concerns reduced press rates to China and Press Wireless Incorporated of Chicago.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on settlement of the 19.8-kilocycle radio-frequency dispute
subfiles.from: Office of the Solicitor, Department of State
subfiles.about: Records Commander Fisher's report that a radio-frequency dispute with a Japanese station had been settled and that diplomatic action should cease.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that Commander Fisher of the Division of Naval Communications telephoned to report an amicable settlement of the dispute with a Japanese radio station over the 19.8-kilocycle frequency. He requested that no further action be taken and that steps be taken to prevent the American Embassy in Tokyo from making representations to the Japanese Government.

interest: The file provides unusually specific evidence about the structure and timing of press cable-rate reductions, including the change from 36 to 18 cents per word and the creation of a 9-cent deferred rate. It also reveals the limits of interdepartmental knowledge: major federal communications and commerce bodies could not confirm information reported through diplomatic channels. The final memorandum adds a distinct example of informal technical diplomacy, showing how a radio-frequency dispute could be settled administratively before formal representations were made to Japan.
